House
HOWS
n. (a dwelling; a household or family; a dynasty; the temple as God's house; the church as God's household; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew bayith and Greek oikos, oikia)
From Old English hūs, common Germanic, a dwelling or shelter. Hebrew bayith and Greek oikos both carry the same threefold reach the English word inherited: the building, the family that lives in it, and the line that descends from it. The Hebrew letter beth, second of the alphabet, is itself the pictograph of a house, and the word forms hundreds of place names — Bethel, the house of God; Bethlehem, the house of bread; Bethany; Bethesda. From oikos English derives economy (the law of the house) and ecumenical (of the whole inhabited house).

Biblical Definition

House in Scripture runs up a ladder of meanings, and the ladder is the doctrine. First it is the dwelling: Noah is told, “Come thou and all thy house into the ark” (Gen 7:1), where the building and the family are one thing. Second it is the household under a head, the unit in which faith is confessed and covenant obedience rendered: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15). Joshua does not poll the household; he speaks for it, which is what headship means. Third it is the dynasty: God refuses David's offer to build Him a house and instead builds David one, “thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever” (2Sa 7:16) — a promise no son of David fulfilled until One rose who does not die. Fourth it is the temple, the house of God, where His name dwells. And fifth, gathering all the others, it is the church: “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15). Peter completes the figure by making the members themselves the material — lively stones built up a spiritual house (1Pe 2:5). What began as shelter ends as the dwelling of God with men.

Webster 1828 Definition

A dwelling; the family or household that inhabits it; the dynasty descended from it; the temple as God's dwelling; and, in the New Testament, the church as the household of God built of living stones.

expand to see more

HOUSE, n. [Sax. hus.] 1. In a general sense, a building or shed intended or used as a habitation or shelter for animals of any kind; but appropriately, a building or edifice for the habitation of man.

2. A household; a family of ancestors, descendants and kindred; a race of persons from the same stock; a tribe. The Lord hath sworn unto David... of the house of Judah.

3. A body of men assembled in legislative capacity; as the house of lords or commons. The English political sense preserves the older idea of a corporate body treated as one.

4. In Scripture, the temple: “My house shall be called an house of prayer.” Matt. 21. And the church, considered as God's dwelling among men.

5. The grave, the long home; and, figuratively, the body as the soul's tabernacle — “our earthly house of this tabernacle” (2Co 5:1), a house pitched for a journey and struck at its end.

Key Scripture

Gen 7:1 — "And the LORD said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation."

Jos 24:15 — "And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

2Sa 7:16 — "And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever."

1Ti 3:15 — "But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth."

Modern Corruption

The household as a governed unit with a head, a table, and a confession has been replaced by the house as a private consumption space — and in the church, the household-of-God image has been traded for the corporation, with the pastor recast as executive and the members as clients.

expand to see more

The biblical house is a small commonwealth: it has a head accountable to God, a confession spoken on its behalf, work and worship under one roof, and children catechized within it (Deu 6:6–9; Eph 6:4). What replaced it is a residence — a place where individuals who share an address sleep, charge devices, and depart to separate lives. The change is not merely sociological; it dismantles the unit through which Scripture ordinarily works. Joshua's “as for me and my house” is unintelligible where no one may speak for anyone. Recovering family worship, the family table, and the father's duty to teach is not nostalgia for an era; it is obedience to a standing command.

The parallel corruption runs in the church. When 1Ti 3:15 calls the church God's house, it sets Paul's whole instruction about elders and deacons in a domestic frame — which is precisely why an elder who cannot rule his own house is disqualified from the greater one (1Ti 3:4–5). The corporate model severs that logic: it measures leadership by attendance, revenue, and brand, and it treats members as a customer base whose preferences set the agenda. A household is governed by a father; a corporation is steered by a market. The regulative principle and plural eldership are the practical guards on this, because both put the house under its Owner rather than its occupants.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bayith (house, household, dynasty, temple) and its place-name compounds Beth-el, Beth-lehem, Beth-any; Greek oikos and oikia, source of oikonomia (stewardship, economy) and oikodomē (edification, building up).

expand to see more

bayith (Hebrew, H1004) — house, household, dynasty, temple; the pun at the centre of 2Sa 7, where David offers to build the LORD a bayith and is told the LORD will build him one instead.

beth- (Hebrew prefix) — the construct form behind Bethel (house of God, Gen 28:17–19), Bethlehem (house of bread), Bethesda, Bethany; the second letter of the alphabet is itself the pictograph of a house.

oikos (Greek, G3624) — house and household; the word in the household baptisms of Act 16:15 and Act 16:33, and in Heb 3:6, “whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence.”

oikonomia (Greek, G3622) — the law or management of a house, whence economy and stewardship; Paul calls his apostleship a dispensation, that is, a stewardship of God's house (1Co 9:17; Eph 3:2).

1689 London Baptist Confession 26.2 and chapter 22 — the particular church as the visible household of God, and family worship as a duty binding on every household head, “in private families daily.”

Usage

"“As for me and my house” is quoted constantly and understood rarely: Joshua is exercising headship, publicly binding a household to the LORD, in a speech whose whole point is that neutrality is not on the ballot."

"The Hebrew pun in 2Sa 7 — David will not build the house, God will build his — is the hinge of the Davidic covenant and the reason Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy."

"Preaching 1Ti 3:15 without its domestic frame flattens it into a slogan about doctrine. Paul's point is behavioural: this is how a man conducts himself inside his Father's house."
